topic: the faked bullet-dent 'proof mark' scam on historic 'bulletproof' armor
title: The 'Bulletproof' Armor Dent That Might Be a 500-Year-Old Fake
description: AI-narrated commentary on the real history of armor 'proof marks' -- the bullet dents 16th and 17th century armorers left on breastplates to prove they were shot-resistant, and how some armorers faked that test with a hammer instead of a gun. Sources below.

hook_candidates.text: Here's a 500-year-old armor scam that still fools people today.
Armor buyers once refused to pay until the maker literally shot the breastplate first.
A 17th-century armorer sold soldiers a lie stamped right into the steel.
How do you prove armor stops a bullet? Sometimes, you just hit it with a hammer.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who owns a replica sword and swears vintage armor could stop a musket ball, because they want to prove that claim was sometimes just a hammer trick.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume that dent in old armor is honest proof it stopped a bullet, not part of a centuries-old scam.
closing_comment: That bulletproof armor dent might be a total fake, since some armorers just hammered one in and skipped the actual gun test entirely. Ever spotted a dented breastplate at a museum?

sources.note: Confirms proof marks are deliberate bullet-test dents left on 16th-17th century breastplates to show firearm resistance.
Academic study finding many 'proof' dents don't match real bullet-impact energy, suggesting fraudulent hammer marks.
Met Museum's surviving shot-proof cuirass, a breastplate and backplate genuinely tested against firearms.
